next_steps: Maya to send Dedicated pricing tiers and seat-level licensing spreadsheet by 2025-10-02
Jared to share benchmark checklist and a small runbook for prewarm/hot-pool testing by 2025-10-03
Customer to provide QPS profile and model sizes (float32/quant) for pilot by 2025-10-06
Schedule a 1-hour pilot kickoff (bench environment + test prompts) for week of 2025-10-13

header:
Date: 2025-09-29 | Start: 16:00 PT | Duration: 52 min
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jared Kim (Redwood SE), Oliver Grant (Head of ML - Skyline), Priya Shah (Infra Lead), Daniel Cruz (CTO)
summary: Discovery call to scope Skyline Labs' needs for reserved/dedicated GPU capacity. Main focus: sizing committed pool, tenant isolation vs shared hot-pool, burst strategy & pre-warm, failover routing to hosted models, and compliance questions (data residency, KMS). Agreed to run a short pilot with dedicated nodes and synthetic traffic to validate latency and cost tradeoffs.
questions: What isolation levels are required for regulated PII workloads?
How fast can we burst and what are cold-start penalties?
What's Redwood's routing policy between dedicated and hosted fallbacks?
How do we measure and cap cost during unpredictable peaks?
transcript:
[00:00] Maya: good afternoon everyone, thanks for joining. this is maya and jared from redwood. can you hear us ok?
[00:08] Oliver: yeah, loud and clear. thanks for doing this. we wanted to get into how dedicated capacity would look for our inference workloads and figure out the burst story.
[00:17] Maya: great. quick round robin — oliver, priya, daniel, can you say roles?
[00:22] Oliver: sure, im oliver, head of ml — we run the inference infra team.
[00:26] Priya: priya, infra lead, focused on networking and our VPC setups.
[00:30] Daniel: daniel, cto, oversight and procurement sync.
[00:34] Jared: thanks. quick agenda — committed sizing, tenant isolation, burst/hot-pool, fallback, compliance, then next steps. sound good?
[00:41] Oliver: yep. to start, our production model mix: 2 LLM families. one small-chat model (around 8B dense) and a larger, retrieval-augmented generation model that peaks at ~50 tokens seq length, uses a KV cache heavily. overall peak qps currently 350 rps but sustained is 80-120, and we get spikes up to ~900 for launches.
[01:05] Priya: and oh — we are hybrid cloud, prefer VPC peering to Redwood private plane when possible. some data must remain in our region east-us-2.
[01:13] Jared: okay. initial thought — a reserved pool sized for your sustained throughput (say 4-6 A100 equivalents) plus a hot-pool for burst. question: do you need strict hardware isolation or is tenancy isolation (dedicated nodes but multi-tenant inside customer) ok?
[01:28] Daniel: procurement wants hard isolation for certain customers — on-prem or full node isolation — but for internal traffic we could do shared dedicated. there is a cost delta.
[01:36] Maya: yep, we typically offer both: dedicated tenancy (full node pinning) and a dedicated shared pool with tenant-level isolation. full-node isolation gives you stronger blast radius containment but increases reserved costs.
[01:47] Oliver: what's the practical impact of the hot-pool approach? we worry about cold starts for the larger model, esp with the KV cache warm-up.
[01:53] Jared: cold-starts: with KV cache and long context, first few requests can add 100-300ms or more depending on model size and whether quantization was used. our hot-pool prewarmed workers keep the KV cache primed for your common prefixes which reduces that tail. hot-pool is an always-on small set of workers that take burst traffic and then autoscale out if needed.
[02:15] Priya: and how fast can it autoscale? we need to know speed and limits — some of our SLAs require <150ms p95 for chat bursts.
[02:23] Jared: scaling time depends on instance boot + model load. for optimized images and quantized models we can scale new workers in ~40-90 seconds; prewarmed hot-pool gives you near-instant capacity. if you need <150ms p95 we recommend sizing for that tail on the reserved pool or use hot-pool with prewarmed workers.
[02:40] Oliver: so for our peak 900 rps bursts we probably need to combine both: reserved for baseline and hot-pool for a portion. can you model cost implications?
[02:47] Maya: yes — we'll send a modeling sheet. quick rule of thumb: reserved capacity covers steady QPS at lowest cost per token; hot-pool and burst instances are billed at on-demand equivalent rates and can add 20-40% to peak month depending on frequency.
[02:59] Daniel: curious about fallback — if hot-pool/ reserved nodes saturate, can requests route to hosted redwood models (lower cost but maybe higher latency)?
[03:08] Jared: yes, routing policies are configurable. you can prefer reserved, then hot-pool, then hosted equivalent with optional model-variant mapping. for sensitive data you can add filters to prevent routing to hosted models.
[03:20] Priya: on compliance — SOC2, KMS, audit logs, SSO. we need SAML SSO and customer-managed KMS for key wrapping.
[03:28] Maya: we support SAML/SSO, and for Private deployments we integrate with customer KMS/HSM. for Dedicated we offer optional KMS integration; audit logs can be exported to your SIEM. we'll include our compliance pack in the follow-up.
[03:40] Oliver: great. can we do a small pilot to validate tail latency and cost? something like 4 reserved nodes + hot-pool with 2 prewarmed workers and synthetic spike tests?
[03:49] Jared: yep, that's the standard approach. pilot duration typically 2 weeks — first week to validate perf and cache warmup patterns, second week to run stress and cost modelling.
[03:58] Daniel: what about model variants and quantization? we plan to run FP16 for core models and int8/4 for some inference paths. any caveats?
[04:06] Jared: quantization reduces memory and model load time but depending on operator support you might see small accuracy drift. the runtime picks kernels depending on quant format; we'll recommend a quant profile per model. important for burst behavior — quantized models load faster so your scale-up time improves.
[04:21] Maya: also worth noting prefetching common KV prefixes during low traffic windows improves perceived latency for the heavy RAG model.
[04:27] Priya: network design — if we do dedicated nodes in east-us-2, we need private connectivity and clear egress paths. do you support VPC peering and private endpoints?
[04:36] Jared: yes, VPC peering and private endpoints supported. for Private deployments we can colocate control plane and data plane per your network. we will work with your networking team on route tables and firewall exceptions.
[04:47] Oliver: monitoring and cost controls — can we set hard caps so we dont accidentally blow budget during marketing spikes?
[04:53] Maya: we have token-based quotas and budget alerts; for Dedicated we can set route-level caps and automatic fallbacks to hosted models or reject new requests once budget threshold hits. we can also enforce quota per API key.
[05:05] Daniel: ok — semantically, procurement will want commitment details: minimum contract term, ability to increase reserved GPUs mid-term, and early-exit clauses.
[05:13] Maya: typical reserved contracts are 12/24 months with mid-term scale-up available (we provision additional nodes with X weeks lead). early exit is handled case-by-case; we'll include standard terms in the pricing doc.
[05:23] Priya: any recommended stress test prompts or benchmark harness you can share?
[05:26] Jared: yes, i'll share a benchmark checklist and a harness we use internally; it includes TTLs for cache, warmup scripts, and a sample payload generator (we'll link it). the harness simulates both constant background load and sudden fan-out spikes.
[05:37] Oliver: can we also log model output and token counts to measure cost per API call?
[05:41] Maya: yes — we provide token-level accounting in the console; for Dedicated we can export detailed traces and per-route cost breakdowns.
[05:48] Daniel: any gotchas we should watch for during pilot?
[05:51] Jared: watch model cold-starts, KV cache miss rates, and network egress costs if you route to hosted during fallbacks. also, quantized vs fp16 differences can change throughput profiles. we'll help tune batch sizes and concurrency.
[06:04] Oliver: sounds good. one other question — in catastrophic failure of a region, do you support cross-region failover for dedicated pools?
[06:11] Maya: yes. you can configure multi-region redundancy. failover may involve cold starts and model loads in the failover region; we recommend a small prewarmed replica in the DR region for critical workloads.
[06:21] Priya: ok i think we have enough to scope a pilot. from our side we'll need the pricing, security pack, and the benchmark harness.
[06:29] Maya: we'll send those. jared will own the bench checklist, ill own pricing and procurement terms.
[06:34] Daniel: timeline wise, procurement wants a pilot in october — target week of oct 13.
[06:38] Maya: noted. we'll target that.
[06:40] Oliver: thanks all.
[06:41] Maya: quick recap of next steps: pricing doc + contract terms, benchmark harness + checklist, customer provides traffic profile and model artifacts, schedule pilot kickoff.
[06:50] Priya: im tagging our networking person into the follow-up thread.
[06:53] Jared: linking the playbook here: https://redwood.com/playbooks/dedicated-burst-v2 (internal) and i'll drop the benchmark checklist in chat.
[06:59] Daniel: perfect. thanks everyone.
[07:02] Maya: thanks — we'll follow up over email and set a calendar for the kickoff. bye.

Notes & imperfections: occasional speaker mislabels (transcription), 'control plane' read as 'control plain' in a couple of spots, KV cache spelled 'K V cache' intermittently.
